intro: You are standing on Tell Atchana, ancient Alalakh, a mound in Hatay province. Its story runs from the 3rd millennium BC to the 12th century BC. This was a Bronze Age city of the Amuq plain, and it is famous above all for one treasure: the cuneiform archive of King Niqmepa. Shall we step back in time?
history: In the 2nd millennium BC, Alalakh was the capital of the kingdom of Mukiš, and with its palaces and temples it was one of the most important centres of the region. Its secrets came back to light when Leonard Woolley excavated the mound between 1937 and 1949. The mound lies just southeast of Tell Tayinat.
structure-1: You are now at the Palace of Niqmepa. This is the palace attributed to Niqmepa, the Late Bronze Age ruler of Alalakh, here at Tell Atchana. Pause for a moment and picture the king whose archive made this mound famous.
structure-2: Next comes the Old Palace, also known as Palace VII. It is the earliest palace building excavated at Tell Atchana — the oldest seat of power uncovered on this mound.
structure-3: Here stand the temples. These sacred buildings mark the region as an important religious centre. Imagine the prayers once spoken within their walls.
structure-5: Now look at the Bronze Age houses. These are the remains of Bronze Age houses at Tell Atchana: beyond the palaces and temples, this is where everyday life was lived.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the city walls.
facts: Did you know? The inscription on the statue of King Idrimi is one of the most important documents of the ancient Near East: an autobiography written in cuneiform, in the first person. King Idrimi had his life story carved onto his own statue in 104 lines — how he lost his throne, fled, and returned. The statue is now in the British Museum. On the palace walls, frescoes were found painted in the technique of the Minoan palaces of Crete, some of the most concrete evidence of the link between the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean. And the cuneiform archive of King Niqmepa records how a small Bronze Age kingdom kept its footing between great powers.
outro: This brings our tour of Tell Atchana, ancient Alalakh, to an end. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited a very long time; let them wait for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
